questions.question: Does the form of arsenic matter more than the total amount?
questions.answer: Yes. Inorganic arsenic (iAs) is the toxicologically dominant form and the carcinogen of regulatory concern, and it is what the wiki's content focuses on ([[sources/efsa-arsenic-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Total-arsenic measurements that do not distinguish inorganic from organic species are not informative for risk, so when you see a "total arsenic" number the actionable question is what fraction is inorganic. Distinguishing them often requires speciation analysis (HPLC-ICP-MS) rather than total-arsenic ICP-MS ([[sources/navaretnam-2025-rice-as-speciation|Navaretnam et al. 2025]]).

questions.question: What foods are the biggest source of inorganic arsenic in the diet?
questions.answer: For people without elevated drinking-water arsenic, rice and rice-based foods are the dominant single dietary source, because rice efficiently accumulates inorganic arsenic from flooded-paddy soils ([[sources/efsa-arsenic-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Brown rice carries more than white rice because the bran layer concentrates the metal ([[sources/su2023-arsenic-brown-rice-benefits-risks|Su et al. 2023]]). Other notable matrices include seaweed (especially hijiki), apple and grape juice, and rice protein powder and rice syrup; finfish is mostly harmless arsenobetaine and poses minimal arsenic-specific dietary risk.

questions.question: Why is inorganic arsenic a health concern, and what are its effects?
questions.answer: Inorganic arsenic is classified as a Group 1 human carcinogen by IARC, with dose-response associations for lung, bladder, and skin cancer at chronic exposures ([[sources/atsdr-arsenic-toxprofile-2007|ATSDR 2007]], [[sources/efsa-arsenic-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Non-cancer effects documented in the literature include cardiovascular effects, neurodevelopmental effects in children, dermal effects such as hyperpigmentation and keratosis, peripheral neuropathy, and emerging diabetes associations ([[sources/atsdr-arsenic-toxprofile-2007|ATSDR 2007]]). Mechanistically it binds sulfhydryl groups in proteins, generates oxidative stress, and inhibits DNA repair rather than forming direct DNA adducts ([[sources/thomas-2021-arsenic-methylation|Thomas 2021]]).

questions.question: Who is most vulnerable to arsenic exposure?
questions.answer: Infants fed rice cereal as a first solid food are a key vulnerable group, which is why the FDA set a 100 ppb action level for infant rice cereal ([[sources/fda-iAs-rice-cereal-2020|FDA 2020]]). Children under three are exposed at 2 to 3 times adult per-kilogram rates because of greater per-kg food intake ([[sources/efsa-arsenic-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). Private-well users in arsenic-affected regions fall outside EPA drinking-water monitoring, and people with low folate or B12 status have reduced methylation efficiency, increasing retention of inorganic species ([[sources/thomas-2021-arsenic-methylation|Thomas 2021]]).

questions.question: What are the regulatory limits for arsenic in water and food?
questions.answer: The EPA drinking-water Maximum Contaminant Level for total arsenic is 10 ppb (10 µg/L), lowered from the earlier 50 ppb standard, and it applies to public water systems but not private wells ([[sources/epa-arsenic-drinking-water-mcl|EPA Arsenic MCL]]). The FDA set a 100 ppb action level for inorganic arsenic in infant rice cereal in 2020 ([[sources/fda-iAs-rice-cereal-2020|FDA 2020]]). Major bodies have declined to set a single tolerable intake: JECFA withdrew its PTWI of 15 µg/kg body weight per week in 2010, and EFSA reports cancer BMDL01 values of 0.3 to 8 µg iAs/kg body weight per day instead ([[sources/jecfa-82nd-arsenic|JECFA 82nd]], [[sources/efsa-arsenic-contam-2009|EFSA 2009]]). ATSDR derives a chronic oral MRL of 0.3 µg As/kg/day anchored on dermal effects ([[sources/atsdr-arsenic-toxprofile-2007|ATSDR 2007]]).

questions.question: How can I reduce arsenic exposure from rice and well water?
questions.answer: For infants, choosing non-rice or rice-minor first cereals such as oat, barley, or multi-grain lowers exposure, since these carry substantially less inorganic arsenic per serving than rice cereal. For older children and adults, white rice carries roughly 50 percent less inorganic arsenic than brown rice from the same source, and cooking rice in excess water that is drained off reduces iAs by approximately 40 to 50 percent ([[sources/su2023-arsenic-brown-rice-benefits-risks|Su et al. 2023]]). Private-well users in arsenic-affected regions should test their water through an EPA-certified lab and treat, substitute, or reduce use if levels exceed 10 µg/L ([[sources/epa-arsenic-drinking-water-mcl|EPA Arsenic MCL]]).
